rationale: The exact entry's core is carried directly by the two printed references: Matt 7:26 supplies the hearer-who-does-not-do as the foolish man, while Ps 14:1 supplies the lawless/corrupt character; both texts and the paired wise/fool contrast exclude mere unintelligence. This is tighter and better attested than the broader common reading of generic practical godlessness, which the same texts already subsume without remainder. No material assertion printed in the entry itself is left unsupported.
book_core_identification: The fool is the one who hears God's word and will not do it (the lawless), not the unintelligent; opposite of the wise.
chapter_only_objections: Extended oil/virgins typology and Gethsemane press reading go beyond the glossary entry
Hebrew-Matthew textual variants and specific oil-purchase mechanics are chapter-only
strongest_counter_interpretation: The biblical fool is the practically godless person who lives as if God does not exist or matter (moral-spiritual rebellion), of which hearing-without-doing is only one illustrative application rather than the definitional core.
counter_core_identification: Practical godlessness / moral-spiritual rebellion against God rather than intellectual deficiency.
material_core_denial: The counter does not deny that the hearer-who-does-not-do is a fool; it only treats that description as non-definitional and secondary to the Ps 14:1 denial-of-God motif.
counter_case: Ps 14:1 / 53:1 opens with the heart-denial of God and immediately links it to corruption and abominable works
Proverbs repeatedly frames folly as despising wisdom/instruction and being right in one's own eyes
Traditional and scholarly consensus treats the moral-religious category as primary across Hebrew terms
book_explanatory_advantages: Jesus Himself supplies the binary definition in Matt 7:24-27: both hear the identical words; the sole difference is doing versus not doing
The entry's 'lawless' gloss unifies Ps 14:1's corrupt works with the Matt 7 sand-builder and the later 'I never knew you' lawlessness verdict
Wisdom texts (Ps 111:10; Deut 4:6) explicitly equate wisdom with doing the commandments, locking the opposite pair
Excludes intelligence without remainder, matching the common consensus while remaining textually precise
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for the full proverbial spectrum (simple, scoffer, hardened fool) under one moral heading
Naturally incorporates the rich-fool and foolish-virgins motifs as further instances of practical ungodliness
